title: Marriage
hook: for some churches a sacrament, for others a covenant; all see it as faithful love

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sabbath economics: rest for everyone, servants included, corners of the field left standing, a jubilee of release. Your line was enough for all. Did a day of buying nothing feel like enough? Day one thousand two hundred sixteen.

Two people stand at the front of a church, hands joined, a little nervous. The words they repeat are old. In the Book of Common Prayer, the groom promises: "to have and to hold from this day forward, for better for worse, for richer for poorer, in sickness and in health, to love and to cherish, till death us do part." The bride's promise runs almost word for word the same. Nobody in the room knows which of those they'll get. That's the point. They promise all of it, in advance. Christians in quite different churches make promises like these, even when they explain what's happening in different words. Today: marriage.

The root is in the opening pages of Genesis: "Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh." Leave, cleave, become one. When Jesus is asked about divorce, he goes straight back to that verse and adds a line still heard at weddings: "What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." So for him, marriage isn't only a private contract. God is the one joining. Here's where churches describe it differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians count marriage as a sacrament: a holy sign through which God's grace is truly given to the couple. In the Catholic understanding, the bride and groom are the ministers of the sacrament to each other. Lutheran and Reformed churches don't number marriage among the sacraments. They call it a covenant, or a holy estate that God created and blesses. A promise, made before God and witnesses, with God as a party to it. Paul, writing to the Ephesians about husbands and wives, says: "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church." That one line holds the common ground. Whatever word a church uses, sacrament or covenant, they agree that a faithful marriage is meant to show something about God: love that chooses the other person again, for better and for worse, and doesn't leave.

Here's the practice: hold one married couple in mind. Settle, and breathe. Choose a couple you know: your parents, grandparents, a friend and their spouse, neighbors, or your own marriage if you have one. Picture them on an ordinary day, not the wedding day. Somebody's tired. Somebody's doing dishes. Think about which of the old vows they're living right now: better or worse, richer or poorer, sickness or health. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just wish them well, specifically. The bell holds the time.
Marriage. For Catholic and Orthodox Christians, a sacrament; for Lutheran and Reformed churches, among others, a covenant before God. For both, faithful love: two becoming one flesh.
Your line: two becoming one. Today, send that couple a short note, or do one small thing that makes their ordinary day easier. Day one thousand two hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Christians marry in church services with vows exchanged before God and witnesses; Catholic and Orthodox churches celebrate marriage as a sacrament, while Protestant churches celebrate it as a covenant or holy estate blessed by God.

myth: every church calls marriage a sacrament
Catholic and Orthodox churches do; Lutheran and Reformed churches, among others, call it a covenant or holy estate.
in Catholic teaching, the couple are the ministers of the sacrament
the bride and groom give the sacrament to each other.
Jesus treats marriage as only a private contract
he says God does the joining: "what therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder."

fork.setup: people come to Jesus with a question about divorce. where does he go for his answer?
options: to the customs of his own day.
back to Genesis: the two shall be one flesh.
fork.reveal: he goes back to the beginning, to Genesis 2:24, and adds: "what therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder."

trapdoor: what you thought: a wedding is a nice ceremony and a legal contract.
what it means: a lifelong promise made before God. a sacrament for some churches, a covenant for others, faithful love for all.
what a scholar hears: Paul calls marriage a great mystery, mysterion in Greek; the Latin Bible rendered it sacramentum.

notes: BCP 1662 vow quoted from memory ('to have and to hold from this day forward... till death us do part'); confirm exact wording and punctuation against the 1662 text.

Catholic teaching that the spouses are the ministers of the sacrament (Latin rite, CCC 1623) is stated; the Orthodox understanding gives a central role to the priest's blessing and crowning, so the 'ministers' line is attributed to Catholics only. Confirm.

'Lutheran, Reformed and other Protestant churches don't number marriage among the sacraments' is a generalization; confirm or soften. Anglican teaching counts marriage among the 'commonly called' sacraments but not the two Gospel sacraments.
Trapdoor: the Vulgate renders mysterion in Ephesians 5:32 as sacramentum; confirm.
Divorce and remarriage, and differing church teaching on who may marry, are left for other days; day 1218 addresses disagreement.

Audit pass: the hook said 'each promises the other' the quoted vow, but in the 1662 BCP only the man's vow reads 'to love and to cherish'; the woman's reads 'to love, cherish, and to obey'. The hook now gives the quoted words as the groom's and says the bride's runs 'almost word for word the same'. Keeper may prefer a modern-rite note.

Editor pass: the review no longer recalls manna (cut from day 1215); the claim about 'other Protestant churches' was narrowed to Lutheran and Reformed churches 'among others' in the teach, word and myth; the fork option 'the latest ruling of the teachers' became 'the customs of his own day' so the teachers of his day are not cast as the foil.
